c_lines: 243 (`limit = cursor = *p;`), 106 (`#define YYFILL(n) do { } while (0)`), 400 and 12 further copies (`if(YYLIMIT == YYCURSOR) YYFILL(1);`), OOB read site 390 (`yy16: yych = *++YYCURSOR;`)
invariant: I1 (T1-universal, diffuse) - every read or write through a pointer lands strictly inside the allocation that pointer was derived from
obligation: I1/O3 primary (a scan whose only stopping condition is an in-band terminator must additionally be bounded by the buffer's known length), plus I1/O2 and I1/O4
mechanism: php_var_unserialize is a re2c-generated lexer driven by a raw `const unsigned char *cursor` that is advanced with `++YYCURSOR` and dereferenced at ~13 sites. Its only bound test is `if(YYLIMIT == YYCURSOR) YYFILL(1);`, and both halves of that test are dead: `YYFILL` is defined at :106 as `do { } while (0)`, and at :243 `limit = cursor = *p;` sets the limit to the START of the buffer rather than to its end, so `YYLIMIT == YYCURSOR` is true exactly once (at the first byte) and false forever after. The true end of the buffer IS in scope the whole time -- `max` is the third parameter of UNSERIALIZE_PARAMETER (:150) -- but it is only ever passed along to recursive calls (:160, :168) and never compared against anything. On a truncated serialized string the lexer simply walks off the end of the zval allocation.
ptr_cursor_evidence: Mechanical count over php_var_unserialize's lexer body (lines 238-420): 7 pointer-deref-with-advance forms (`*++YYCURSOR`, `*(YYMARKER = ++YYCURSOR)`), 0 `arr[i]` index forms. The cursor is a bare `const unsigned char *`; there is no index variable in the function at all.
benign_behaviour: On a well-formed serialized string it lexes the type tag, the length/count fields and the payload, and returns a decoded value. A natural u64 checksum for an extracted kernel: fold each accepted token's (type_tag, length, payload byte sum) into a rolling 64-bit hash, plus the final cursor displacement `cursor - start` and the number of tokens accepted. That last term is exactly the quantity the defect corrupts.
adversarial_trigger: Any serialized string truncated mid-token. Corpus ships input/crash/CRASH-066.php: `unserialize('O:3:"obj":1:{')` -- the object body is announced as having 1 element and the buffer ends immediately after the `{`, so the lexer keeps advancing past the terminator looking for the element. Reproducer present.
self_containment_detail: The re2c state machine (~700 lines of generated `yyNN:` labels) is verbatim-portable and needs nothing but a byte pointer, but it dispatches into zval construction. A narrowed extraction keeps the lexer, the parse_iv2/parse_uiv helpers (:117-148, themselves unbounded pointer walks) and the YYFILL/YYLIMIT/limit=cursor defect exactly as written, and replaces the zval actions with checksum accumulation. Nothing about the defect lives in the parts you drop.
blob_drivability: Excellent, and directly: the blob IS the serialized byte string. No opcode encoding needed -- the flat blob is fed as `*p` with `max = p + len`, and the driver loop calls the kernel once per blob. Benign blobs are generated by an ordinary serializer; adversarial blobs are the same bytes truncated at a random offset.
hotness: Hot on real traffic: unserialize() is on the session-read path of every PHP application that uses the default session serializer, so it runs at least once per authenticated request on WordPress/phpBB. It is a per-request parser, not a per-loop kernel.
mechanism_distinctness: The bound exists as a live variable in scope and is simply never consulted -- distinct from url-scheme-fixed-offset-peek (where no length is passed at all past the entry) and from unserialize-blind-fixed-advance (where a check exists but the advance jumps over it).
risks: The extraction must NOT quietly set `limit = *p + len`: that is the fix, and doing it during extraction turns the kernel benign. The `limit = cursor = *p` line must be copied verbatim. Second risk: a re2c lexer over a NUL-terminated blob will often stop by accident on the terminator byte, so the harness must place the blob without a trailing NUL (or with adversarial bytes after it) or the defect will look unreachable.

c_lines: 141 (`ee = s + (len == 45 ? 60 : (int) floor(len * 1.33));`), read/write loop 143-148, tail reads 158-166, terminator write 168
obligation: I1/O2 primary (an index or offset must be validated against the block's own length, not against a separately-tracked variable), plus I1/O1 and I1/O3
mechanism: php_uudecode allocates the output as `emalloc(ceil(src_len * 0.75) + 1)` (:131) -- correct for well-formed uuencoded data -- and walks the input with a bare `char *s` against the true end `e = src + src_len` (:133). The loop `while (s < ee)` then reads `*s, *(s+1), *(s+2), *(s+3)` and advances `s += 4` regardless of `e`, and writes three bytes per iteration through an entirely unbounded output cursor `p`. A one-byte line that declares length 45 sets `ee = s + 60` over a 4-byte input: 15 iterations of a 4-byte read and a 3-byte write past both ends. Two further defects sit in the same function: :158 `if ((len = total_len > (p - *dest)))` assigns a boolean to `len`, making the `len > 1`/`len > 2` tails at :160/:162 dead and dereferencing `*s` when `s == e`; and :168 `*(*dest + total_len) = '\0'` writes at the sum of the *declared* lengths, which is unrelated to the allocation.
ptr_cursor_evidence: Mechanical count over php_uudecode (lines 126-171): 17 pointer-deref-with-offset/advance forms (`*(s + 1)`, `*(s + 2)`, `*(s + 3)`, `*p++`, `*s++`, `s += 4`), 0 `arr[i]` index forms. Four separate cursors (`s`, `e`, `p`, `ee`) and no index variable anywhere in the function. This is the single densest pointer-offset walk among all 47 spatial rows.
benign_behaviour: On correct uuencoded input it decodes 4 base-64-ish characters to 3 bytes per group, honours the per-line length byte, skips the newline, and returns the decoded byte count. u64 checksum: FNV-fold the decoded output bytes and mix in `total_len` and the number of lines consumed.
adversarial_trigger: A line whose declared length byte overstates the bytes actually present. Corpus ships input/crash/CRASH-115.php: `convert_uudecode("M" . str_repeat("A", 3))` -- 'M' decodes to len 45, so `ee = s + 60` over 3 remaining bytes. Reproducer present, and this row is one of the 8 in my set with crashes_pristine_5_0_0 = True.
emalloc_dependent: false -- the allocation `ceil(src_len*0.75)+1` is computed correctly in double/size_t and is never large; the defect is a loop bound, not a sizing overflow. Substituting plain malloc changes nothing.
self_containment_detail: php_uudecode is 46 lines and depends on exactly two macros (PHP_UU_DEC, PHP_UU_ENC), `emalloc`, `floor` and `ceil`. It can be lifted with no modelling at all.
blob_drivability: Excellent and direct: the blob is the uuencoded byte string, passed as (src, src_len). No wrapper needed. Benign blobs come from the sibling php_uuencode in the same file (:80-124), which gives a free generator for correct inputs.
hotness: None documented. convert_uudecode is a rarely-called library function, not a request-path kernel. This candidate's value is mechanism quality, not frequency.
mechanism_distinctness: The loop bound is derived from a length field *inside the data* rather than from the buffer; both an over-read and an over-write flow from the same wrong bound. Distinct from iptc-guard-sized-for-short-branch (which has a bound check that is merely too small) and from the sizing-wrap family (where the allocation, not the loop, is wrong).
risks: The corpus's CWE for this row is CWE-125 and its root_cause_id says 'writes past emalloc'; both an OOB read and an OOB write occur and an extraction must not silently pick one. `floor(len*1.33)` is floating point -- an extraction that replaces it with integer arithmetic changes which `len` values trigger the overrun and must be justified. The output cursor `p` has NO bound at all, so under ASan the write fires before the read on most inputs.

c_lines: 132 (`if (*(e + 5) == ':')`), with the same-family peeks at 125 (`*(e+2)`), 128 (`*(e+3)`); the unused true end is computed at 94 (`ue = s + length;`)
obligation: I1/O1 primary (must not read at or beyond the end of the block the pointer names), plus I1/O3

The probe is also the wrong offset for its own purpose (`file:///c:` puts the colon at e+5 only when the drive letter is one character), so it is both an over-read and a logic bug.
ptr_cursor_evidence: Mechanical count over php_url_parse_ex (lines 85-297): 5 pointer-deref-with-offset forms vs 2 `arr[i]` forms. The function declares `char const *s, *e, *p, *pp, *ue;` -- five cursors and one `int length` that the scheme block ignores. `*(e+2)`, `*(e+3)`, `*(e+5)` is the literal spelling the idiom census names as the missing shape.
benign_behaviour: On a real URL it splits scheme/host/port/user/pass/path/query/fragment. For a kernel, the output is naturally a checksum over the seven (offset, length) component spans -- fold `(component_index, start_offset, span_length)` for each recognised component into a u64. Ordinary URLs from a request log give a stable benign workload.
adversarial_trigger: Any URL of the exact shape `file://` + one or two more characters -- the buffer must end between e+3 and e+5. Corpus ships input/crash/CRASH-110.php: `parse_url("file:///")`. Reproducer present. Note crashes_pristine_5_0_0 is False: it is a one-byte over-read that a plain build absorbs; ASan is what makes it visible.
self_containment_detail: The whole of php_url_parse_ex is ~210 lines and needs `estrndup`, `strchr`, `strncasecmp` and `php_replace_controlchars`. A narrowed extraction keeps the scheme block (:96-148) verbatim -- that is where both url.c defects live -- and replaces `estrndup` component capture with span recording. `php_replace_controlchars` is a 5-line loop and can come along verbatim.
blob_drivability: Excellent: the blob is the URL bytes plus its length, exactly as the C receives them. One subtlety that is itself part of the pattern: the C mixes a `length` parameter with `strchr`-style NUL termination, so the harness must decide whether the blob is NUL-terminated. Both choices are faithful to some caller; the pristine caller (PHP_FUNCTION(parse_url)) passes a NUL-terminated zval, so a NUL-terminated blob is the honest default and is what makes the +5 land one past the end.
hotness: Hot: parse_url is called on every URL an application handles; the ASan-on-real-traffic census directory (.temp/san_tests/) is the place to confirm frequency, but the function is on the ordinary request path of any app that rewrites links.
mechanism_distinctness: A blind constant-offset peek forward from a found cursor, with the buffer length present but unread. Distinct from url-length-not-decremented-cursor-desync (same function, but that one is a length/pointer bookkeeping desync, not a peek) and from unserialize-blind-fixed-advance (which advances the cursor rather than peeking).
risks: The over-read is exactly one byte and lands on the allocator's own padding in a plain build, so a kernel that does not run under a redzone-checking harness will see nothing. The `strncasecmp("file", ret->scheme, sizeof("file"))` at :127 compares 5 bytes including the NUL against a heap string -- if the extraction shortens the scheme capture, this guard changes behaviour and the +5 path stops being reachable.

c_lines: 190 (`req_size = *pos + MAX(min_width, copy_len) + 1;`), 192-198 (the doubling loop and erealloc), 206-208 (pad write, CRASH-001 sink), 211 (`memcpy(&(*buffer)[*pos], add, copy_len + 1);`, CRASH-011 sink); feeding sites 443 (`register long num = strtol(...)`), 483 (`int alignment, width, precision, ...`), 614/626 (long-to-int store)
invariant: I11 (T1-universal, diffuse) - every size, index and count is the true mathematical value of its expression at each step
obligation: CRASH-001: I11/O1 + I11/O3 (a size expression must not wrap; the bytes reserved must be at least the bytes requested). CRASH-011: I11/O2 + I11/O3 (a size must not be narrowed to a type that cannot represent it, and must not be permitted to become negative). Both contribute I1/O1.
mechanism: One guard at :192, `if (req_size > *size)`, is the only thing standing between the format arguments and three unbounded write loops, and two different attacker-controlled integers can make it false. (a) The width path: `php_sprintf_getnumber` returns `long` from an unbounded `strtol` (:443) into the `int width` at :483, and :190 computes `req_size = *pos + MAX(min_width, copy_len) + 1` in `int`. A width near INT_MAX wraps req_size negative, the buffer is never grown, and the right-pad loop at :206-208 then writes `npad` bytes one at a time. (b) The precision path: the same `long`-to-`int` store makes `precision` = INT_MIN for the literal 2147483648, `expprec` is set, so `copy_len = MIN(max_width, len)` = INT_MIN at :180, `npad` is clamped to 0, `MAX(min_width, copy_len)` picks min_width, req_size stays tiny and the guard is satisfied honestly -- and then :211 does `memcpy(dst, add, copy_len + 1)` with a length of INT_MIN+1, which as `size_t` is ~1.8e19.
ptr_cursor_evidence: Mechanical count over php_sprintf_appendstring (lines 171-218): 0 pointer-offset-deref forms and 0 `arr[i]` forms; the writes are spelled `(*buffer)[(*pos)++]`, an index through a pointer-to-pointer. The cursor is the `int *pos` out-parameter, not a pointer. Index-family, not the census idiom.
benign_behaviour: It appends `add` to a growing output buffer, right- or left-padded to min_width with `padding`, truncated to max_width when expprec is set, and advances `*pos`. For a kernel: run a sequence of (min_width, max_width, padding, alignment, payload) records out of the blob and checksum the final buffer bytes plus `*pos` and the number of reallocs performed. The realloc count is a good second output because it is exactly the quantity the guard controls.
adversarial_trigger: CRASH-001: a format with a literal prefix and a near-INT_MAX width, e.g. `sprintf("XXXX%2147483646d", 1)`. CRASH-011: `sprintf("%.2147483648s", "x")`. Both reproducers ship (input/crash/CRASH-001.php, CRASH-011.php) and both rows are crashes_pristine_5_0_0 = True.
emalloc_dependent: false for both. In CRASH-001 the wrap is in the `int req_size` expression in the caller and erealloc is never reached at all -- the buffer is simply not grown. In CRASH-011 the wrap is in `int copy_len` and the huge value goes to memcpy, not to the allocator. Neither defect touches `unsigned int real_size`; substituting plain malloc changes nothing. (The secondary `while (req_size > *size) *size <<= 1;` at :193-195 CAN drive a negative *size into erealloc, and that path WOULD be allocator-sensitive, but it is not the path either reproducer takes.)
self_containment_detail: php_sprintf_appendstring is 48 lines with a 12-argument signature and depends only on `erealloc`, `memcpy`, MIN/MAX and ALIGN_LEFT/ALIGN_RIGHT. php_sprintf_getnumber (:439-452) is 14 lines. Both lift with no modelling. The 400-line php_formatted_print driver around them is NOT needed.
blob_drivability: Excellent, via the p27-style opcode route: decode the blob into a stream of append records (min_width u32, max_width u32, padding byte, alignment bit, expprec bit, payload length + bytes) and call the kernel once per record against a persistent (buffer, pos, size) triple. The buffer that grows inside the kernel is precisely the p27 shape.
hotness: Hot: sprintf/printf/vsprintf are among the most-called PHP functions on any page render, and php_sprintf_appendstring is called once per conversion specifier plus once per literal run.
mechanism_distinctness: Two attacker-controlled integers defeat ONE guard by opposite routes -- signed wrap of the sizing sum vs. narrowing of a parsed long to a negative int. Distinct from the char_to_str/chunk_split family, where the wrapped value is handed to the allocator and the allocator obliges with a short block.
risks: This is the only entry where I merged two corpus rows, and they are genuinely two mechanisms sharing a function and a guard -- if the extraction only reproduces the memcpy sink it silently drops CRASH-001, and if it only reproduces the pad loop it drops CRASH-011. The 12-argument signature invites simplification; `neg`, `always_sign` and the :200-205 sign-injection block mutate `add`, `len` AND `copy_len` after the guard has been evaluated, so dropping them changes which inputs trigger. The reproducer .php comments cite php-4.0.2 line numbers (:183, :187) and a 4.0.2 guard spelling `(*pos + max_width) >= *size`; the pristine 5.0.0 spelling is `req_size > *size` at :192 and the CSV's :190/:207/:211 are the correct 5.0.0 citations.

obligation: I1/O1 primary (must not read before the start of the block the pointer names), plus I1/O2
mechanism: The ZEND_ISEMPTY string-offset handler bounds-checks a signed index with a single one-sided comparison: `offset->value.lval <= Z_STRLEN_PP(container)`. `lval` is a `long` carrying the user's array subscript, so any negative subscript passes the test trivially and is then used directly as a byte index into the string buffer. `empty($s[-1000000])` reads a megabyte before the allocation. The comparison is also off by one on the upper side (`<=` where `<` is meant), which reads the string's own NUL -- benign in PHP because zvals are NUL-terminated, which is exactly why the lower-bound hole survived: the visible symptom of the upper bound is nothing at all.
ptr_cursor_evidence: A single `buf[i]` index expression. Index-family. Included deliberately as the minimal spatial control against which the pointer-cursor rows are compared.
benign_behaviour: For an in-range subscript it answers 'is this byte of the string zero/absent' and returns a bool. Kernel form: read (offset i64) records from the blob, evaluate the guarded index against a fixed haystack, and fold each boolean answer plus the loop counter into a u64.
adversarial_trigger: A single negative subscript. Corpus ships input/crash/CRASH-145.php: `$s = "abc"; var_dump(empty($s[-1000000]));`. Reproducer present; crashes_pristine_5_0_0 = True, and it SEGVs a plain build, not just an ASan build.
self_containment_detail: Three lines. The only thing to model is 'a string zval' = (ptr, int len), which any kernel already has.
blob_drivability: Excellent and trivially: the blob is a header (haystack length + haystack bytes) followed by a run of little-endian i64 offsets. Every offset is a kernel iteration. This also gives a clean knob for benign-vs-adversarial mix ratio, which most of the other candidates do not have.
hotness: Hot: this is a Zend VM opcode handler (ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_DIM_OBJ), executed once per `isset()`/`empty()` on a subscript. `isset()` is one of the most-executed constructs in PHP application code.
mechanism_distinctness: A one-sided bound check on a signed index -- the smallest possible spatial defect, and the only candidate in the set with no arithmetic, no cursor and no allocation. It is the natural floor of the ladder against which everything else is priced.
risks: The kernel is so small that at -O2 the compiler may hoist or vectorise the whole loop, and a bounds check added at any rung may be free. That is a finding, not a problem, but the harness must be able to see it. Second risk: the upper-bound off-by-one reads the NUL terminator and is only a defect if the extraction does NOT NUL-terminate the haystack -- the pristine behaviour depends on the zval's guaranteed NUL, so the honest extraction keeps it and reports the `<=` as a latent, non-firing half of the same defect.

c_lines: 240 (`if (((unsigned) start + (unsigned) len) > len1) { len = len1 - start; }`), declarations at 208-209 (`int len1, len2; long start, len;`), end-pointer construction at 245-248, fault surface at 1330-1336 (php_strspn)
obligation: I11/O2 primary (a size must not be narrowed to a type that cannot represent it), plus I1/O1 and I1/O3
mechanism: `start` and `len` are `long` (64-bit) but the clamp at :240 evaluates them as `(unsigned)`, i.e. 32-bit. A `len` of 2^32 becomes 0 under the cast, the clamp `((unsigned)start + (unsigned)len) > len1` is false, and `len` keeps its full 64-bit value. The unclamped value is then turned into a raw end pointer, `s11 + start + len`, and handed to php_strspn as `s1_end`. php_strspn terminates on pointer EQUALITY (`for (spanp = s2; p != s1_end && spanp != s2_end;)` at :1330) while advancing with `c = *(++p)` at :1332, so a bogus `s1_end` is not merely a wrong limit -- it is a limit the walk can step straight past, and the walk then runs until it faults. The defect is a narrowing cast in a check; the sink is an unbounded pointer walk two functions away.
ptr_cursor_evidence: Mechanical count over php_strspn/php_strcspn (lines 1324-1360): 2 pointer-deref-with-advance forms (`*spanp++`, `*(++p)`), 0 `arr[i]` forms. Both functions take their bounds as END POINTERS (`char *s1_end, char *s2_end`) rather than as lengths, and terminate on `!=` rather than `<` -- the census idiom in its most fragile spelling.
benign_behaviour: Returns the length of the initial span of s1 consisting only of bytes in the mask s2. Kernel: blob supplies (haystack bytes, mask bytes, start, len) records; checksum the returned span lengths.
adversarial_trigger: `strspn($s, $mask, 0, 4294967296)` with a mask that contains a NUL byte, so the walk does not stop on the haystack's own terminator. Corpus ships input/crash/CRASH-102.php with exactly that, including the NUL-in-mask detail. Reproducer present.
emalloc_dependent: false -- the truncation is a `(unsigned)` cast inside a comparison in the extension, and no allocation is sized from it. Substituting plain malloc changes nothing.
self_containment_detail: php_strspn is 13 lines, php_strcspn ~15, and the clamp block from php_spn_common_handler (:224-248) is 25 lines. All three lift with no dependency beyond the zend_parse_parameters call, which the blob decode replaces.
blob_drivability: Excellent: (haystack len, haystack, mask len, mask, start i64, len i64) records straight out of the blob. The i64 fields are exactly where the adversarial input lives, so benign and adversarial blobs differ only in two eight-byte fields.
hotness: Moderate: strspn/strcspn are library calls, not request-path kernels, but php_strcspn is also used internally by the string functions. No ASan-census evidence gathered.
mechanism_distinctness: The check is right, the types under the check are wrong -- a narrowing cast written INTO the guard by the author, not an accidental overflow. Distinct from the appendstring family (where the guard's arithmetic wraps) and from substr_compare (where the guard is short-circuited away entirely).
risks: The truncation only exists because `long` is 64-bit and `unsigned` is 32-bit; an extraction that picks matched-width types makes the defect vanish. The type widths ARE the pattern here and must be pinned explicitly. Second risk: the `p != s1_end` walk will run for ~4 GiB before it faults on a real machine, so the kernel needs a smaller but equally-truncating pair of widths (e.g. u16 clamp over a u32 length) or a mapped guard page, and either choice is a deviation that must be recorded.

mechanism: The parser keeps a byte cursor `s` and a remaining-length counter `length` and must keep them in step by hand. At :118 the idiom `length -= ++e - s;` is correct because `s` still holds the old start. At :143 the SAME line is wrong, because :139 already advanced `s` to `e + 1` four lines earlier: `++e - s` is therefore 0 and `length` is not decremented at all. The cursor has moved forward and the counter has not. `goto just_path` then recomputes the buffer end from the desynced pair, `ue = s + length` (:167), placing `ue` past the true end by exactly the number of bytes `s` advanced, and :292 does `estrndup(s, ue - s)` -- a read of the full original length starting from a position inside the string. For `parse_url('a:/')` the copy runs off the end; for a longer scheme it runs off by the scheme length.
ptr_cursor_evidence: Same function as url-scheme-fixed-offset-peek: 5 pointer-offset-deref forms vs 2 `arr[i]`, five `char const *` cursors, and the defect itself is pointer arithmetic (`++e - s`) feeding a length variable. This is the census idiom's characteristic failure -- a length maintained alongside a cursor instead of derived from it.
benign_behaviour: Identical to url-scheme-fixed-offset-peek: component spans of a parsed URL. Same u64 checksum over (component_index, start_offset, span_length).
adversarial_trigger: A URL whose scheme is followed by `:/` and whose scheme is not `file`, e.g. `a:/` or `mailto:/x`. Corpus ships input/crash/CRASH-073.php: `parse_url('a:/')`. Reproducer present.
emalloc_dependent: false -- `estrndup(s, ue-s)` allocates the right amount for the length it was given; the defect is that the length is wrong, and it is wrong by a small positive amount, so no allocator behaviour is involved.
self_containment_detail: Same extraction as url-scheme-fixed-offset-peek -- the two defects live 11 lines apart in the same function, so ONE narrowed extraction of php_url_parse_ex carries both. Reported separately because the C mechanisms are different and the manager may want them as separate rows.
blob_drivability: Excellent, same as url-scheme-fixed-offset-peek: the blob is the URL bytes plus its length.
mechanism_distinctness: A hand-maintained length counter drifts out of step with the pointer it shadows, and a later `base + length` reconstruction of the end pointer inherits the drift. Distinct from every other candidate: no overflow, no missing check, no wrong constant -- a correct line copied to a place where its precondition no longer holds.
risks: NEAR-DUPLICATE of url-scheme-fixed-offset-peek at the file and function level (not at the mechanism level) -- if the manager builds php_url_parse_ex once, these are two triggers of one kernel, and the report must not double-count them as two patterns. Second risk: the over-read length equals the scheme length, so a one-character scheme over-reads by two bytes and will be invisible without a redzone; the adversarial blob should use a long scheme.

c_lines: 2946 (`Z_STRLEN_P(result) = len + (char_count * (to_len - 1));`), 2947 (`emalloc(Z_STRLEN_P(result) + 1)`), counting pass 2935-2939, emitting pass 2950-2965 with the OOB write at 2957
obligation: I11/O1 + I11/O3 primary (a size expression must not wrap; the bytes reserved must be at least the bytes requested), I1/O1 contributing
mechanism: A textbook two-pass size-then-emit. The counting pass at :2935-2939 walks the input with `source < source_end` and counts occurrences. The sizing line at :2946 then computes `len + char_count * (to_len - 1)` entirely in `int`; with 65536 occurrences and a 65537-byte replacement the product is exactly 2^32 and wraps to 0, so the result length is reported as the INPUT length and :2947 allocates that. The emitting pass at :2950-2964 then walks the same input and writes through `target`, an output cursor with no bound of any kind -- neither a limit pointer nor a remaining-bytes counter -- so it faithfully writes the ~4.3 GB it was always going to write into a 64 KB block. mechanism: The only bounds check on `offset` is `if (len && offset >= s1_len)` at :4786, and its first conjunct disables it: when the optional `length` argument is absent or zero, `len == 0` and the check is skipped entirely, for BOTH directions. `offset` is a `long` and is never clamped, so `s1 + offset` at :4794 can be formed arbitrarily far before or after the string. The length passed alongside it, `s1_len - offset`, becomes larger than the string when offset is negative, and `cmp_len` is computed as `MAX(s2_len, s1_len - offset)` cast to `uint`, so the comparison is told to read a span that starts out of bounds and is longer than the buffer. Three separate quantities -- the base pointer, the remaining length and the compare length -- are all wrong, all because one guard was made conditional on an unrelated argument.
ptr_cursor_evidence: The function itself has no cursor; it forms `s1 + offset` once and hands it off. Index/pointer-construction family.
benign_behaviour: Compares up to `length` bytes of two strings starting at `offset` in the first, returning <0/0/>0. Kernel: (s1, s2, offset i64, len i64, cs flag) records; checksum the comparison results.
adversarial_trigger: A large negative offset with the length argument zero. Corpus ships input/crash/CRASH-108.php: `substr_compare("aa", "a", -99999999, 0, 0)`. Reproducer present, crashes_pristine_5_0_0 = True.
self_containment_detail: 13 lines plus `zend_binary_strncmp`, which is a `memcmp` plus a length-difference tiebreak. Nothing to model.
blob_drivability: Excellent: (s1 len, s1, s2 len, s2, offset i64, len i64, cs u8) records. The two i64 fields carry the whole adversarial surface.
hotness: Low: substr_compare is a rarely-used application-level function.
mechanism_distinctness: A bounds check made conditional on an argument that has nothing to do with the bound, so an ordinary default value silently turns the check off. Distinct from string-offset-signed-index-no-lower-bound (where the check is unconditional but one-sided) and from strspn-clamp-truncated-by-32bit-cast (where the check runs but on truncated values).
risks: NEAR-DUPLICATE at the invariant level with string-offset-signed-index-no-lower-bound (both are 'a signed offset reaches before the buffer'), but the C mechanisms differ: one guard is one-sided, the other is short-circuited. The manager may want only one. Second risk: `MAX(s2_len, (s1_len - offset))` mixes `int` and `long` operands, so the promotion rules matter to which branch of MAX wins -- an extraction that normalises the types changes which quantity ends up in `cmp_len`.
